title: Runtime TypeScript Execution Tools
subtopics: Understanding supported syntax and tool limitations
learning_outcomes: Explain runtimes and typescript runners in the context of runtime typescript execution tools.
Apply the lesson concept in a small TypeScript example and describe what the compiler can check.
Identify one limitation or failure case and choose an appropriate runtime check or test when needed.

content.intro: Learn runtime typescript execution tools through a compact mental model, syllabus-aligned subtopics, a worked example and a practical task. The goal is not to memorize syntax but to know what the type contract guarantees and what evidence is still needed.
content.why_it_matters: Code that touches browser APIs, files, networks, environment variables, or JSON needs runtime and environment awareness. The declared type is not proof that an external value is valid.

content_blocks.title: Mental model
content_blocks.text: **Runtime TypeScript Execution Tools.** This lesson belongs to **Packages, Ecosystem, and Developer Tools**. Start by identifying the problem that runtime typescript execution tools solves. In TypeScript, separate three questions: what values your program intends to accept, what the compiler can prove from the code, and what must still be checked while the program runs. The last category matters whenever data comes from a user, file, API, storage layer, or an untyped JavaScript dependency.

content_blocks.title: Syllabus topics and how to use them

items.title: Runtimes and TypeScript runners
items.text: For runtimes and typescript runners, treat incoming values as untrusted until runtime checks establish the required shape. A TypeScript annotation does not validate network, file, database, storage, or user-provided data by itself.

items.title: Type stripping versus type checking
items.text: For type stripping versus type checking, connect the concept to a small concrete example, state the assumption it relies on, and verify the result with a compiler diagnostic or a runtime test as appropriate.

items.text: For understanding supported syntax and tool limitations, make the toolchain/configuration explicit and reproducible. Check the configured TypeScript version and use the project command so your result matches the course assumptions.

content_blocks.title: Example: Runtime TypeScript Execution Tools
content_blocks.expected_output: These are example scripts only. Install and configure the named tools in the project, pin compatible versions, and do not assume every tool supports every compiler release.
content_blocks.run_instructions: This course displays TypeScript examples as static teaching text. The CodeLeaf web playground currently previews HTML/CSS/JavaScript only; TypeScript is not compiled or executed in the browser preview. This test example expects Vitest in a local disposable project; install it with `npm install --save-dev vitest` and run `npx vitest run` after saving the example as a test file. For actual compiler feedback, create a local project with a pinned TypeScript version and run `npx tsc --noEmit`. For snippets requiring a browser, Node.js, React/JSX or a test runner, use the matching environment and dependencies.
content_blocks.reset_steps: The lesson example does not modify files or remote systems. If you run it locally, use a disposable project directory, keep package versions recorded, and remove only the generated output you created.
content_blocks.limitations: Static lesson example only. The browser preview is not a TypeScript compiler and does not execute backend, Node.js, React/TSX, test-runner, network or filesystem examples.

content_blocks.title: Compile-time versus runtime
content_blocks.text: Type annotations and most type declarations are erased when TypeScript emits JavaScript. They do not validate external JSON, authorize a user, sanitize HTML, or prevent runtime failures by themselves. Validate trust-boundary inputs and test the behavior.

content.task: Create a small TypeScript example for “Runtime TypeScript Execution Tools”. Demonstrate runtimes and typescript runners, explain your assumption, and include one check that shows the expected behavior. Do not treat a type annotation as runtime validation for external input.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example demonstrates at least one syllabus subtopic named in this lesson.
The type contract is explicit enough that another learner can explain what it accepts and rejects.
The learner records a failure case and distinguishes compile-time checks from runtime validation.
hints: Start with the syllabus item “Runtimes and TypeScript runners” and define the smallest example that demonstrates it.
Ask which part is checked by TypeScript and which part depends on runtime data, the environment or a test.
For external input, start with unknown and validate the required shape before using a domain type.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating a successful type check as a runtime guarantee.
common_mistakes.why: Type annotations do not generally validate data after JavaScript starts running.
common_mistakes.fix: Add runtime checks for external input and tests for meaningful failure cases.

common_mistakes.problem: Using any or an assertion to silence a useful diagnostic.
common_mistakes.why: That can hide the exact mismatch the type system would otherwise report.
common_mistakes.fix: Prefer a more precise type or unknown plus narrowing; use assertions only when a verified invariant justifies them.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a compiler setting or runtime example without checking the project environment.
common_mistakes.why: Module resolution, DOM/Node globals, JSX and tool behavior depend on the configured versions and environment.
common_mistakes.fix: Pin the toolchain, match tsconfig to the runtime/bundler, and run the actual project's typecheck and tests.

summary: Runtime TypeScript Execution Tools is taught through the subtopics listed in the source syllabus: Runtimes and TypeScript runners, Type stripping versus type checking, Understanding supported syntax and tool limitations.
Prefer precise contracts and use compiler diagnostics as evidence, not as a replacement for runtime tests.
Validate untrusted data and describe environment/version assumptions explicitly.
